newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU prepared for television shoot-out.
newsitem.headline: EU prepared for television shoot-out.

text.p: European Union governments and the European Parliament seem destined for a Wild-West style showdown next month over plans to revise the 15-nation bloc's broadcasting rules.

The parliament's key Culture Committee made confrontation more likely this week when it maintained calls for stricter limits -- opposed by EU governments -- on the number of Hollywood films and programmes shown on television screens in the Union.

If the full parliament follows the committee's advice in Strasbourg on November 13 -- and that could prove to be the unknown twist in the tale -- there could be a bloody climax to one of the EU's most protracted sagas.
In EU-speak that climax would be called "conciliation", when both sides go to the negotiating table and seek to hammer out their differences.

On the surface the question is how to revise the EU's 1989 Television without Frontiers directive, which said that tv stations should, but only where practicable, devote 51 percent of their screen time to European productions.
The parliament, under intense lobbying by French filmmakers and aware that the EU's film industry is struggling, wants that provision made mandatory.
EU governments say they believe tougher quotas are not the answer and agreed to leave the 1989 law exactly as it is.
But it is not just a question of cinema.
Underlying the storyline is the European Parliament's desire to be taken more seriously and have "co-decision" powers it received under the Maastricht treaty actually amount to something.
The parliament has taken the EU culture ministers' rejection of its position as a slap in the face.
As in many films, it may be possible to predict the ending -- regardless of who are the goodies or the baddies -- and the parliament is a certain loser in the shoot-out.
If the issue goes to conciliation and the two sides fail to agree, the EU law will remain as it is -- exactly what the governments want.
For that reason, EU officials say, some parliament deputies may, when it comes to the vote next month, prefer to side-step a showdown to avoid an inevitable defeat.
The parliament's Culture Committee has also demanded tougher rules for advertising and a firmer definition of broadcasting, to include teleshopping but not the Internet,
It says the amount of advertising during a feature film should not exceed 15 percent of the film's duration.

The committee also wants rules to ensure that broadcasters which receive exclusive rights to screen important sports events like the Olympic Games or the football World Cup do not prevent people from following the events live.
